episode_thesis: Mark argues that asset relationships are conditional on the regime (volatility, monetary/fiscal, sentiment), so a trend follower with macro awareness gets an edge from decomposing regimes, detecting change points and modelling causal networks rather than mining factors. In early 2026 he sees metals and softs as possibly past a bubble peak (hard-to-value assets plus narrative plus excess money), a rotation away from US assets as uncertainty makes them relatively less safe, and a fiscal-versus-monetary tussle whose outcome depends on the new Fed chair. Alan Dunne supplies market evidence and counter-readings (AI narrative flip, EM credibility, Warsh's political flexibility) and both back trend following over years, not months.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Mark says regime awareness is the edge but gives no evidence of out-of-sample benefit; hidden Markov models and change-point detection identify regimes only after the break.
VIX 25 and 40 thresholds are quoted without data, and the claim that 40 is always a peak is stated as certainty.
Mark criticises the factor zoo and ML overfitting while also advocating regime decomposition and network models, which have a large specification space and no stated validation.
The bubble call is hedged: Mark says 'I'd like to say' a peak was hit and later that it is hard to say whether this is a pause or the start of deflation.
Two readings of the payroll revisions are offered (weaker economy needing a hotter run vs lower labour supply) with no resolution.
Retail-driven gold is proposed (Alan) while central banks of sanction-fearing countries are also cited (Mark); the relative weights are not quantified.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs named that lead future prices: the VIX level and direction, stock-bond correlation and inflation, trade/geopolitical/monetary uncertainty indices, the Fed chair's balance-sheet and rate path, Treasury auction absorption (about $700bn in a week), EM versus US inflation and real yields, ETF versus central-bank gold flows, and break points in cross-market network connections. Horizons are months for bubble deflation and years (five) for trend following.
reader_inferences: (reader) Mark's regime decomposition (price, policy-structural, sentiment) can be read as three observable layers: VIX and trend state, fiscal/monetary stance, and uncertainty indices.

(reader) His bubble recipe (excess money plus narrative plus hard-to-value plus constrained supply) gives a checklist that could be coded for commodity peak risk, but both peak calls are about the recent past and not testable from the talk.
(reader) Alan's contribution is mostly market-evidence checks (retail ETF flows, sector inconsistency) that qualify rather than refute Mark's thesis.
(reader) The Warsh disagreement shows the unresolved forward input: whether balance-sheet reduction or lower policy rates dominates, which maps to opposite signs for liquidity-sensitive assets.
